newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Chidambaram to meet RBI on capital inflows.
newsitem.headline: India's Chidambaram to meet RBI on capital inflows.

text.p: Indian Finance Minister P. Chidambaram was quoted on Friday as saying he would meet the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) board on March 15 to discuss foreign capital inflows and their impact on the value of the rupee.
Chidambaram told the Times of Indian newspaper in an interview that he advocated the further opening up of the Indian market to consumer goods imports.
The finance minister was asked if he had a strategy for managing a possible "deluge" of foreign capital inflows in the 1997/98 fiscal year starting on April 1.
"The rupee has appreciated in real effective exchange rate terms. A large inflow of foreign exchange will result in appreciation of the rupee and this will cause some problems," he said.
"I am going to Bombay to meet with the RBI board on March 15. We will discuss it there."
Chidambaram was asked if a viable option for using up some of the foreign exchange inflows was to open up India's market for consumer goods imports.
"It is viable and necessary to open up consumer goods imports. Opening up of imports is good in itself. It is an advance on trade policy," he said.
Chidambaram said liberalisation of consumer goods imports would help boost India's "sluggish" import growth and increase customs revenue.
"Therefore, I would advocate further liberalisation of the import policy," he said.
Chidambaram was asked to name the crucial areas in which the government would have to "deliver" in 1997/98.

He said: "keeping money supply and inflation under control, keeping expenditure under a tight leash, ensuring that amounts earmarked for planned expenditure are spent fully and effectively, and kickstarting the telecom and petroleum sector now that full-fledged policies are in place".

He acknowledged apprehensions among leftwing parties in the 15-party governing coalition over the revival of public sector firms and a proposed opening up of the insurance sector. But he said he believed the Left would go along with his proposed policies.
The finance minister said he saw no reason why the government would not reach its 1997/98 tax revenue targets despite large tax rate cuts.
